title: A spinning top, held at its tip and precessing under gravity
abstract: A spinning top, held at its tip and precessing under gravity.
situation:
### The objects

| name | shape | given properties |
|---|---|---|
| `pivot` **(static)** | `point` | `mass = 1`, `position = [0, 0, -0.6]`, `inverse_mass = 0` |
| `top` | `cylinder` | `mass = 1`, `radius = 0.42`, `half_height = 0.06`, `position = [0, 0, 0.6]`, `velocity = [0.6122448979591837, 0, 0]`, `angular_velocity = [0, 1.0204081632653061, 20]` |

Each row is one rigid body. The simulator computes each body's inertia tensor from its shape; you never type an inertia tensor in.

### The shapes, and the inertia each implies

**`point`** — a massive point: it has mass but no size and no inertia. `I = 0`. A point cannot store rotational energy, so no torque turns it. Used for anchors, for planets whose size does not matter, and for charges. A `point` with `inverse_mass = 0` is the standard way to bolt a mechanism to the world.

**`cylinder`** — a uniform solid cylinder. `I_zz = m r^2 / 2` about the axis of symmetry, and `I_xx = I_yy = m (3 r^2 + 4 h^2) / 12` about any diameter. Symmetric about its LOCAL z axis, like every round shape here. A long thin cylinder is a rod; a short fat one is a disc.

### What each property means

- **`mass`** — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- **`position`** — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- **`inverse_mass`** — one over the mass. Setting it to **0** makes the body STATIC: no force can accelerate it. This is how a body is bolted to the world, and it is representable as a finite number, which infinite mass is not.
- **`radius`** — the radius, in metres.
- **`half_height`** — half the height along the cylinder's own z axis.
- **`velocity`** — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.
- **`angular_velocity`** — the spin rate `omega`, as `[wx, wy, wz]` in radians per second, in WORLD axes. Setting it sets the angular momentum to `L = I omega`, which is what is carried.

### The interactions

- **Mutual gravity is OFF** (`g_constant = 0`). The simulator's default is 1, so this had to be said explicitly; without it, bodies that are supposed only to bounce or to be held by joints would also attract each other.
- **Uniform gravity** is `[0, -3.0, 0]` metres per second squared, applied to every body alike.
- **Contact is OFF**. Nothing here is meant to touch anything else, so the rootfinder is not armed.
- **1 joint** holds the bodies together. A joint is an exact geometric relation held for all time by constraint forces the solver computes — not a stiff spring.
eom:
There are 2 bodies. Each obeys Newton's and Euler's equations, both of which are **second order**:

```
m_i * d2(x_i)/dt2 = m_i g + J^T lambda

I_i * d(omega_i)/dt + omega_i x (I_i omega_i) = T_i
```

The `omega x (I omega)` term in Euler's equation is the gyroscopic term. It is what makes a tumbling body's spin axis wander even with no torque at all, and it is why rigid-body motion cannot be reduced to three independent rotations.

The forces on the right are:

- `m_i g` — the uniform field, here `g = [0, -3.0, 0]`
- `J^T lambda` — the constraint forces the joints generate. These are NOT written down by you: they are the Lagrange multipliers, solved for at every step so the joint equations hold exactly

and the torques `T_i` likewise carry a constraint part `J_omega^T lambda`, which is how a bearing resists being twisted out of line.
constraints:
**1. `ball pivot top` — 3 rows.** The two bodies share one point, and may turn any way about it. Three equations, one per coordinate of the shared point: `g = (x_a + R_a r_a) - (x_b + R_b r_b) = 0`, where `r_a` and `r_b` locate the pivot in each body's own frame. No axis is given, because a ball joint has no preferred direction.

**The arithmetic that decides whether this can be solved at all.** 1 non-static body gives `6 x 1 = 6` degrees of freedom, against **3 constraint rows**, leaving `6 - 3 = 3` freedoms.

Those remaining freedoms are the motion the mechanism actually has. Some of them may be passive — a freedom nothing applies a force along simply stays where it started.

Every row is held at the position level (`g = 0`) **and** at the velocity level (`d(g)/dt = J u = 0`) at the same time. That is what the GGL formulation is for, and it is why these joints do not slowly come apart.
reduction:
**Sizing this particular problem.** There are 2 bodies, so the state vector `y` has

```
2 bodies x 13 numbers = 26 components
```

laid out as consecutive 13-number blocks in creation order, each holding position (3), linear momentum (3), orientation quaternion w-first (4), and angular momentum (3).

The 1 static body still occupies its 13 slots. Its inverse mass is zero, so its momentum-to-velocity map returns zero and it never moves — carried as constants rather than special-cased out of the layout.

On top of those 26 differential unknowns are the algebraic ones: one Lagrange multiplier `lambda` and one position-level multiplier `mu` for each of the 3 constraint rows, so

```
3 lambda + 3 mu = 6 algebraic unknowns
```

giving **32 unknowns in total**, solved as one implicit system.

**What is handed to the Rust SUNDIALS translation.**

Because there are joints this is a DAE, and `METHOD IDA` selects the pure-Rust translation of **IDA**. IDA is handed a residual of the implicit form

```
F(t, y, y') = 0
```

built from four blocks: the position rows carrying the `-M^-1 J^T mu` correction, the momentum rows carrying `+J^T lambda`, the rows `g(q) = 0`, and the rows `J u = 0`. IDA runs its variable-order variable-step BDF method and calls back into that residual; the Newton solve at each step is what determines the constraint forces.

**Tolerances.** This model has a joint that grips ORIENTATION, and such a joint imposes a floor of `rtol = 1e-6` and `atol = 1e-8` however tight a tolerance you ask for. That is not timidity: the index-2 accuracy ceiling is real, and asking for more produces convergence failures rather than better answers. Every joint except `CONSTRAIN` grips orientation.

**Consistent start.** A DAE cannot start from an arbitrary state: the start must satisfy `g = 0` and `J u = 0` together. If the initial velocities are not compatible with the joints — a body turning about an offset pivot must have its centre moving — the simulator projects them onto the nearest compatible set and reports how much it changed them.

steps.title: Set up the world
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 4 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set system.rtol = 1e-5` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `rtol` is the integrator's relative error tolerance. Smaller is more accurate and slower. Joints that grip orientation impose a floor of `1e-6`, because the index-2 accuracy ceiling is real and asking for more produces convergence failures rather than better answers.

The value expected here is `1e-5`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.atol = 1e-7` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `atol` is the integrator's absolute error tolerance, which is what governs components passing near zero, where a relative tolerance means nothing. Orientation joints impose a floor of `1e-8`.

The value expected here is `1e-7`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.g_constant = 0` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `g_constant` is the gravitational constant `G` used for the mutual attraction between every pair of bodies, `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`. **Its default is 1, not 0**, which catches people out: bodies rattling in a box also attract each other unless you say otherwise. Set it to 0 for a mechanism or a collision experiment; set it to a real value for an orbit.

The value expected here is `0`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.uniform_gravity = [0, -3.0, 0]` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `uniform_gravity` is a uniform gravitational field applied to every body, as `[gx, gy, gz]` in metres per second squared. This is the everyday 'g' of falling, entirely separate from the mutual attraction above.

The value expected here is `[0, -3.0, 0]`. A successful `set` prints nothing.
steps.code:
sim.do("set system.rtol = 1e-5")
sim.do("set system.atol = 1e-7")
sim.do("set system.g_constant = 0")
sim.do("set system.uniform_gravity = [0, -3.0, 0]")

steps.title: Set up the world (2)
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`collide off` disarms contact detection. Nothing in this model is meant to touch anything else, so leaving it on would have the solver arm a rootfinder hunting for impacts that never happen. The form is `COLLIDE [ON|OFF]`; with no argument it reports the current setting.

It prints the resulting state and the number of collidable pairs.

steps.title: Create the bodies
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> The pivot is a POINT, so its inertia is the zero matrix and it cannot
> turn: a genuine fixed support. A sphere with inverse_mass = 0 would
> still be free to spin, and the ball joint would drive it.

The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`new point` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a massive point: it has mass but no size and no inertia**, named `pivot`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I = 0`. A point cannot store rotational energy, so no torque turns it. Used for anchors, for planets whose size does not matter, and for charges. A `point` with `inverse_mass = 0` is the standard way to bolt a mechanism to the world.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 1` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `position = [0, 0, -0.6]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- `inverse_mass = 0` — one over the mass. Setting it to **0** makes the body STATIC: no force can accelerate it. This is how a body is bolted to the world, and it is representable as a finite number, which infinite mass is not.

Because `inverse_mass` is zero this body is **static**: no force can move it. It is part of the world, not part of the motion.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.
steps.code: sim.do("new point as pivot { mass = 1, position = [0, 0, -0.6], inverse_mass = 0 }")

steps.title: Create the bodies (2)
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> The joint pivots at the MIDPOINT of the pair, so the support at
> -0.6 and the centre of mass at +0.6 put the tip exactly at the origin.
> A cylinder is symmetric about its LOCAL Z axis, so body z is the
> symmetry axis and no rotation has to be applied to aim it.

The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`new cylinder` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a uniform solid cylinder**, named `top`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I_zz = m r^2 / 2` about the axis of symmetry, and `I_xx = I_yy = m (3 r^2 + 4 h^2) / 12` about any diameter. Symmetric about its LOCAL z axis, like every round shape here. A long thin cylinder is a rod; a short fat one is a disc.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 1` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `radius = 0.42` — the radius, in metres.
- `half_height = 0.06` — half the height along the cylinder's own z axis.
- `position = [0, 0, 0.6]` — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- `velocity = [0.6122448979591837, 0, 0]` — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.
- `angular_velocity = [0, 1.0204081632653061, 20]` — the spin rate `omega`, as `[wx, wy, wz]` in radians per second, in WORLD axes. Setting it sets the angular momentum to `L = I omega`, which is what is carried.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.
steps.code: sim.do("new cylinder as top { mass = 1, radius = 0.42, half_height = 0.06, position = [0, 0, 0.6], velocity = [0.6122448979591837, 0, 0], angular_velocity = [0, 1.0204081632653061, 20] }")

steps.title: Declare the joints
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`BALL` declares a joint. Its form is

```
BALL <a> <b>
```

and it contributes **3 scalar constraint equations** to the system, leaving 3 of the 6 relative freedoms between the two bodies.

What it holds: the two bodies share one point, and may turn any way about it.

Three equations, one per coordinate of the shared point: `g = (x_a + R_a r_a) - (x_b + R_b r_b) = 0`, where `r_a` and `r_b` locate the pivot in each body's own frame. No axis is given, because a ball joint has no preferred direction.

Here it is applied to `pivot top`. The pivot goes at the **midpoint of the two bodies' centres as they stand right now**, and is then remembered in each body's own frame — which is why bodies are positioned before they are joined. The command prints a confirmation naming the joint and its row count.

steps.title: Choose the integrator
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`method ida` chooses the time integrator. The form is `METHOD <adams|bdf|sprk|ida>`.

Here it selects the pure-Rust translation of **IDA**, SUNDIALS' implicit differential-algebraic solver. Any model with a joint MUST use it, and the simulator refuses every other method for such a model rather than silently integrating an unconstrained problem.

All stepping in this simulator goes through the vendored pure-Rust SUNDIALS translation. There is no hand-written Euler or Verlet anywhere.

discussion:
**What the cells above actually established.**

- The values printed above are the result. Read them against the physical expectations set out earlier in this notebook.

**How to judge a number here.** A disagreement with theory is only a defect if it fails to shrink when you ask for more accuracy. Tighten `system.rtol` and `system.atol` and re-run: a discretisation error converges, and a bug does not. The one place this does not apply is a model with orientation-gripping joints, where `rtol` is floored at `1e-6` and tightening past it buys nothing.

**The full note from the example this notebook pairs with**, which sets out why it was built this way:

A spinning top, held at its tip and precessing under gravity.

pivot --BALL-- top

A BALL joint holds one point and frees all three rotations, which is
exactly what the tip of a top is. Three rows on one free body: six
freedoms in, three left, and they are the three the top needs.

THE CLOSED FORM. A symmetric top spinning at w3 about its own axis,
with its centre of mass a distance r from the pivot, precesses about
the vertical at

Omega = M g r / (I3 w3)

This is usually quoted as the FAST-TOP approximation, good when the
spin swamps the precession. It is not an approximation here. The
exact condition for steady precession at tilt theta from the vertical
is

M g r = Omega I3 w3 - I1 Omega^2 cos(theta)

and this top is mounted with its axis HORIZONTAL, theta = 90 degrees,
so the cos(theta) term is exactly zero and the simple formula is
exact. That is why the axis lies along z and gravity along -y.

The numbers, all of them chosen so the answer is checkable:

M = 1, r = 0.6, g = 3, radius 0.42  ->  I3 = M R^2 / 2 = 0.0882
w3 = 20                             ->  Omega = 1.0204081632653061
precession period = 2 pi / Omega    =  6.1575 s

The recording runs 6.2 s, so you see one full turn and a little more.
Measured over it: the precession comes out 1.020440 rad/s against the
exact 1.020408, three parts in 100,000, and the axis stays horizontal
to 4.3e-5 -- it does not nutate at all.

IT DOES NOT NUTATE BECAUSE IT WAS STARTED ON THE STEADY SOLUTION, and
that takes both velocities, not just the spin. Give the top only its
spin and release it, and it is not on the steady orbit: it dips and
bobs its way around, and the AVERAGE precession misses the formula by
7.8% at this spin rate. To start it steady, the whole body must also
be turning about the vertical through the pivot:

angular_velocity = [0, Omega, w3]      spin, plus precession
velocity         = [Omega * r, 0, 0]   the centre of mass on its circle

Both together are a rigid rotation about the pivot plus a spin about
the symmetry axis, and the pivot itself stays still under both, so
g_dot = J u = 0 exactly and nothing is projected at the start.

THE TOLERANCE. As in the rod-chain recording (grammar §12.9), a
recording is one `step` per frame and every `step` is a cold restart.
A gyroscope turning at 20 rad/s is the most demanding scene here: the
automatic orientation-joint floor of 1e-6 / 1e-8 is NOT enough, and
the restarts fail at t = 1.12. This is the one scene that has to go
looser than the floor, which the solver's own error message suggests.
